task: Write one sentence of your own using the word wizened. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know wizened should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The bristlecone's wizened trunk, two thousand years of wind-carved knots, is barely wider than a fence post.
Dried has simply lost its moisture — it stops short of wizened, which has shrunk and creased along the way.
Mummified goes further than wizened: nothing is left but a preserved husk.

Shriveled means shrunken and wrinkled from lost moisture, and it is age-neutral — a balloon, a grape, or yesterday's peeled orange can shrivel in a day. Wizened adds the signature of long time: slow drying that leaves hands, faces, and orchard apples creased. Anything can be shriveled; only the aged look wizened.

Gnarled means knotted and twisted, like old wood or arthritic knuckles — the shape itself has warped. Wizened is about drying and shrinking: moisture gone, surface creased, size reduced. An oak root can be gnarled yet full of sap; a wizened apple twists nowhere but shrinks and creases.

The old verb wizen survives only inside this participle — nobody today says a plum 'wizens' on the counter, and the root built no other English words. One caution while you're here: wizened has nothing to do with wise or wizard; the resemblance is pure coincidence.
Wizened means dry, shrunken, wrinkled.
Appalachian apple dolls get their wizened faces from the fruit itself: carved fresh, then left to dry for a month until the cheeks pucker into an old woman's smile — the shrinking does the sculpting.
Wizened is the precise word because it names all three changes at once — dried out, shrunken, and creased.
Wrinkled alone could describe damp laundry; wizened tells you moisture left slowly and took size with it, the signature of long age.
Wizened is for living things and once-plump produce — elders, hands, apples, roots — dried and creased by time.
Shriveled is the plainer, age-neutral word; gnarled adds twisting, as in old wood.
And resist the sound-alike trap: wizened means dried by age, not made wise by it.

The climbing museum's favorite photograph shows the guide Tenzing Bhote at twenty-five, round-cheeked and grinning under a felt hat.
Beside it hangs the portrait taken on his ninety-second birthday.
The face in the second frame is wizened: shrunken close to the bone, creased in every direction, browned by seventy years of high-altitude sun.
Yet visitors say the two photographs are unmistakably the same man — the grin has not moved.
A caption quotes his granddaughter: the mountains worked on him slowly, she says, the way weather cures timber, and made him harder to break.
